strengths: LPAM addresses a practical stitching problem: residual local misalignment can prevent seam cutting from finding an acceptable transition. Targeted patch realignment offers a useful modular extension to existing pipelines without retraining.

Tables 1–2 show consistent improvements across 79 image pairs, four seam-cutting methods, and five alignment methods, including UDIS++. For example, REW plus baseline seam cutting improves SEAGULL SSIM from 0.638 to 0.697 with LPAM.
Figures 1, 5, and 7 illustrate visible repairs. The parameter ablations and explicit failure discussion help explain the tradeoff between local alignment and preserving surrounding structures.
The pipeline is understandable, established components and public datasets are attributed, and Algorithm 1 and the provided code link support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central evidence gap concerns final mosaic quality. Equations (6)–(9) measure agreement between image patches along the selected seam, leaving distortions and patch-boundary artifacts elsewhere largely unmeasured. Table 3 demonstrates this mismatch: removing sigmoid modulation improves RMSE, SSIM, and ZNCC on all three datasets, although Figure 3 shows undesirable artifacts. An independent perceptual assessment or evaluation of structural continuity across the complete mosaic is needed to establish the benefit of the proposed boundary treatment.

The originality claims exceed the demonstrated distinction from prior work. Section 2 already describes seam-guided warp refinement in SEAGULL [22] and dense-matching-based seam/warp estimation in [35], making the subsequent characterization of previous methods as operating on settled pre-aligned images too broad. Localized post-processing is a plausible contribution, but matched quantitative quality and runtime comparisons against these closely related approaches are missing; Figure 7 provides only a limited qualitative comparison.

The seam-quality gate in Section 3.2 can accept a uniformly poor seam: if every error equals a large constant c, max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) still holds and LPAM performs no repair. This exposes dependence on initial alignment having only localized failures. The claim of dissociating seam quality from initial alignment should be narrowed, and this failure regime should be evaluated.

The claimed smooth boundary integration is not guaranteed by the formulation. At beta = 8, Equation (5) gives f(0) approximately 0.018 and f(1) approximately 0.982; moreover, an x-dependent ramp does not enforce compatible displacement along the top and bottom patch boundaries. Fixing graph-cut boundary labels preserves source assignments but does not establish geometric continuity. The actual boundary handling and frequency of introduced artifacts need clearer validation.

The efficiency claim needs qualification. Table 4 reports LPAM's additional processing time separately: on SEAGULL, baseline seam cutting takes 4.11 seconds and LPAM adds 7.34 seconds. This can be acceptable for offline stitching, but the experiments do not establish an efficiency advantage over comparable refinement methods or characterize scaling with image and patch size.

Reproduction from the supplied manuscript remains incomplete: alignment-patch padding and overlap handling, SIFT-flow settings, image resolutions, and acquisition/release details for the new 20-pair dataset are unclear. The code link is helpful, but these choices materially affect alignment quality, boundary behavior, and runtime.
